We will move by Councillor Donauer and seconded by Councillor Ford. Is anyone opposed? That carries. Does anyone have a conflict of interest to report for tonight's public hearing? Not seeing any. Can I get a mover for adoption of the minutes? Moved by Councillor Dubois and seconded by Councillor Parker. Is anyone opposed? And that carries. Councillor Jeffries, can you hear me? Okay. Thank you. Welcome to the public hearing. You go directly to 5.1.1.1, the proposed rezoning at 1411 11th Street West. And I'll turn it over to Mr. Dawson. So we're just on a point of business to be directed. We do first reading of the bylaw. Okay. Thank you. Who would like to move first reading of the bylaw? Thank you, City Clerk Dawson. Moved by Councillor Donauer and seconded by Councillor Timon. Is anyone opposed? That carries. Please proceed. All right. Thank you, Mayor Block. Good evening to you and to City Council. My name is Darrell Dawson, manager of the Development Review section with the City's Planning and Development Department. This public hearing is to consider an application from Prairie for and Wallace Insights to rezone 1411 11th Street West from R2 low-density residential district to RM2 medium-density multi-unit dwelling district.

1411 11th Street West is located in a Holiday Park neighborhood. The site is highlighted on the screen. The site on 11th Street is adjacent to 11th Street and Avenue and South and is developed with a one-unit dwelling. The proposed amendment, if approved, would allow for the development of a multi-unit dwelling consisting of six units. This site is not located in the corridor growth area or within the city's transit development area, which is tied to the Housing Accelerator Fund amendments, allowing for increased density in those areas. Just a note, the nearest boundary of the transit development area is five blocks to the north on 17th Street. The Housing Accelerator Fund amendments approved in June of 2024 did include amendments to the zoning bylaw that provided for the development of a four-unit dwelling as of right in residential zoning districts. And that would apply to this site as it is currently zoned.

In evaluating the proposed amendment, administration considered the relevant policies of the official community plan related to infill development. From administration's review, it has been determined that this proposal does not align with policies for neighborhood infill, particularly as the rezoning would provide for development that would not be compatible with the height and scale of buildings on the block. A detailed policy review is included in our report in Appendix Four. In March of 2024, we did start consultation on this application. Notice was sent out to registered property owners within 150 meters of the site, the ward councillor, and the Holiday Park Community Association. Content was placed on the city's engage page. From that consultation, we heard from 75 residents. 69 of those indicated concern, and six responses indicated support for the application. Of the 69 that had concerns, the concerns noted were: impact on increased density, accommodating on-site waste disposal, increased parking and traffic, impact on the adjacent crosswalk that's right on the corner of 11th Avenue, and impact on the character of the neighborhood and precedent for future zoning.

Based on that feedback, the development review group held a public information meeting. That was held in May of 2024, on May 9th, to provide residents an opportunity to ask questions of the applicants. The developer group and the applicants were present, as well as administration, to answer questions on process. We had 29 residents attend that meeting. Concerns that we heard that night were very much similar to what we had received previously through written correspondence. Following the engagement process, administration met with the applicants to discuss concerns received and to determine if they would consider making revisions to their application. They advised that they wish to proceed with the application as submitted, requesting to rezone the site to RM2 district.

At the Municipal Planning Commission meeting held last month, the applicants noted one of the reasons they are pursuing the rezoning is to obtain favorable financing, which they would not receive if they were to build a four-unit dwelling. Administration wants to note that considering the applicant's business model was not able to be considered in our recommendations. It is also noted that this is a large corner site, and it could accommodate the development. It should be noted that this isn't even the largest lot on the block; there are larger sites on this block and within the area. Larger sites can also be created through consolidation of sites. Approving a rezoning simply because this is a large site could set a precedent for other sites, even though there is no policy or regulations that support that approach.

We want to note that when council was considering the Housing Accelerator Fund amendments in 2024, there was a public hearing two days long. During that meeting, the community spoke loudly about their concerns with increased density. Those concerns were balanced with the growth plans for the city and the Housing Accelerator Fund requirements, which is how the policy and zoning changes were arrived at and adopted. One of the concerns we heard at that time was the worry that developers would continue to push for further increased density than what was approved at that time. Community expectation is that that would not be allowed. This is what is being requested by the applicant, allowing greater density to areas outside of those imposed through the Housing Accelerator Fund amendments.

Administration is fully supportive of applications for infill development where they do align with policy, and you'll see that at the next public hearing. As this application, the rezoning of 1401 113 West from R2 District to RM2 District, does not align with the policies for neighborhood infill and increased densities as approved under the Housing Accelerator Fund amendments, administration is recommending the application be denied. We want to note this is similar to the recommendation and reasons presented during last month's public hearing for the application for 13383 West. Thank you, Mayor Block. Thank you, Mr. Dawson.

Are we okay to go to the public presentations before we ask questions of administration? Okay, so we will go. I'm going to consider that a public presentation, but thank you. The Municipal Planning Commission is up next, Mr. Harley. All right, thank you. Good evening, Your Worship and members of council. My name is Craig Harley, Chair of the Municipal Planning Commission. Thank you for having me this evening. The Municipal Planning Commission, at its regular meeting held on March 31st, 2026, considered a report of the Community Services Division regarding a proposed rezoning of 1401 113 West. During discussion, the commission was informed that administration's review focused on compliance with the official community plan and related evaluation criteria, and that the subject site is located outside of the transit development area and corridor growth area. Administration responded to questions regarding spot zoning, zoning consistency and precedent, building height, traffic assessments, commercial waste requirements, and individual targets. Building height allowances between R2 and RM2 were noted as 8.5 meters and 10 meters respectively. The commission heard presentations from the developer and the representative of the Holiday Park Community Association. The commission was advised that the intent of the developer is to pursue a six-unit residential development and that additional units were necessary for financial feasibility. The applicant indicated that they understood an application for straight rezoning to be a better option and that rezoning by agreement was not pursued due to the investment required. The applicant noted that parking and waste facilities could be accommodated on site and that engagement with the Holiday Park Community Association and city administration had occurred to address concerns. During discussion, the commission was informed that delays in processing the application were due to requests for revision to the proposal from administration and a subsequent period during which the application was not actively advanced by the applicant. The commission heard from a representative of the Holiday Park Community Association who spoke in opposition to the application, citing concerns that the proposed six-unit development was out of character with the neighborhood and raised issues related to precedent density on small lots, on-street parking, traffic safety near school, crosswalks, waste storage, snow removal, and neighborhood livability. After discussion, the motion was made to support administration's recommendation of denial of the proposed rezoning of 1401 11th Street West. The motion was defeated in a vote, although not unanimously. The Municipal Planning Commission did not perform any alternative motions for consideration by City Council. I'd be happy to answer any questions of Council this time.

Thank you, Mr. Hurley. We have questions of Municipal Planning Commission.

Councillor Dubois: Thank you, Madam Chair. Through you, Mr. Hurley, you said the vote was not unanimous. Can you tell me the split, please?

Mr. Hurley: Yes, through your worship, the vote was six opposed, four in favor of administration's recommendation.

Councillor Dubois: So, four in favor of administration?

Mr. Hurley: Yes, four in favor that the application be denied.

Councillor Dubois: So, then, it lost then, didn't it, if it's six to four?

Mr. Hurley: Yes.

Councillor Dubois: So, in favor of the recommendation, it's six against?

Mr. Hurley: Yes. So, through your worship, essentially the commission is not supporting administration's recommendation that the application be denied.

Councillor Dubois: So, you are not supportive. Okay, thank you very much. Appreciate that.

Mr. Hurley: Of course.

Chair: Don't see any other lights on and don't, sorry, go ahead, Councillor Robert Pearce.

Councillor Robert Pearce: All right. Were there any relevant factors that were predominant in the people who voted against it?

Mr. Hurley: Through your worship, the prompt factors would have been general support for infill housing and development. Although outside of the quarter growth area and transit development area, they felt that this application did warrant consideration by Council in favor.

Councillor Robert Pearce: Okay, thank you. And I'll just add a couple of questions. Mr. Hurley, I'm not that it necessarily exactly matters, but did I hear seven to four or six to four?

Mr. Hurley: Through your worship, it was six opposed, four in favor.

Councillor Robert Pearce: Sorry.

Mr. Hurley: Six opposed to the recommendation and four in favor. Yes.

Councillor Robert Pearce: Can you tell me whether or not your commission considered precedents that, as administration has pointed out, we have had a lot of change that has been introduced into the city and that residents are looking for some certainty based on the new rules that we have? And if we keep going outside those rules, how that was considered or what was the process on that?

Mr. Hurley: Through your worship, the, I guess the precedents of these rezoning applications, whether the commission thinks they should be approved or not. We are an advisory committee to City Council. Our decision doesn't hold as much weight as the yes or no from Council. I know you take us very seriously, but I feel like we are quite split with applications of this type of favor or recommending denial. I don't think precedents is that much of a concern for Planning Commission as we are largely a representative of community members, if that answers your question.

Councillor Robert Pearce: Okay, all right. Thank you. I appreciate that.

Chair: And I don't see any of the lights on. So thanks very much for your presentation and for all the work that you do on behalf of the residents of our city. As a volunteer, we really appreciate it. We're going to go now into public presentations. We'll start with Alan Wallace. And I'm sure Mr. Wallace knows this, but for everyone else, just to make sure that the rules are clear, we allow five minutes per speaker. And at the four-minute mark, the yellow light comes on and then you have one minute left. And when the red light goes off, it makes a loud noise. And I'm not allowed to let you say anything else after that. Sorry. Go ahead, Mr. Wallace, it's just yourself when you're ready.

Alan Wallace: Okay, great. Thank you, Your Worship. And I see the PowerPoint is on the screen. But before I start, I just want to mention, although I'm listed as an applicant, I'm not part of the development team. I've just been hired to assist them in the rezoning process. So I just wanted to make that clear. But thank you, Your Worship and members of Council. My name is Alan Wallace with Wallace Insights. And I've been assisting pray for developments in this rezoning. While we can appreciate the administration's concerns regarding compatibility and character of neighborhoods, we feel strongly that it's a misplaced concern in this case. I want to offer the following points. On the screen, I've got several points, although we're going to be very brief. Firstly, this rezoning does conform with the policies contained in the city's Official Community Plan. OCPs are intended to guide zoning and land use decisions. That's correct. The OCP states, however, that each neighborhood in Saskatoon should contain a range of housing and a diversity of housing types. New neighborhoods designed and built today each contain a far greater range of housing types than Holiday Park has without negative effects. If you drive through Aspen Ridge, you drive through Hampton Village, you drive through Brayton, you will see multiple dwellings much larger than a six-plex adjacent to single-family homes all over the city in our new neighborhoods. Secondly, need and demand. The city's most recent housing needs assessment states that at a minimum, Saskatoon will require an additional 5,874 new dwelling units to satisfy housing demand in our city by the end of 2027. Pray for is offering to build quality, attractive housing units at 1401 11th Street West. Next, it is a large site, as has been mentioned. It's over 19 meters wide. Four-plexes are now allowed on sites which are 15 meters wide. So 1401 has over 4 meters of extra width, making it eminently suitable for a larger dwelling unit. Furthermore, it's 32% larger than the minimum site area required in the RM2 district for a six-unit dwelling. So if this was already an RM2 site and you wanted to build a six-plex, this has 32% more site area than the minimum required. A full review of the site's infrastructure was undertaken by the Infrastructure Department. There were no concerns with regards to water. There are no concerns with regards to sanitary sewer capacity. A review of this application was also conducted by the Transportation Department, and there are no concerns with regards to traffic impacts, roadway capacity, or parking. Those comments all came back after the review. In terms of access, this site is served by three roadways: a collector street in the front on 11th Street, a local street at the side, and a rear lane. So three roadways are flanking the site. Regarding speculation, what we mean here is that if the rezoning is approved, the owners can't slip the property to another builder who would build maybe an eight-plex or something higher than a six-plex. The RM2 zoning is capped at six units and no more. And finally, compatibility is deemed in the report, for the recent zoning changes to allow four units as of right have been in effect now for some time. This means that any site with a 15-meter frontage could have a four-plex built on it. The graphic to the right on the screen shows the properties which could have four-plexes built on them. They have at least 15 meters of frontage. As you can see, much of the block could be comprised of four-plexes in the near future. The rezoning of this corner site is really about two dwelling units, two additional dwelling units of 1401. I'll just have you go to the next slide, if you wouldn't mind please. You probably have to tap it a few times to get through the check marks. There you go. Thank you. The final slide shows a random collection of typical four-plex and six-plex designs. They're just randomly placed on the screen. I think it's accurate to say that it's difficult to differentiate between a four-plex and a six-unit dwelling, or a four-unit dwelling and a six-unit dwelling. It's only an additional two dwelling units. So, we feel we're compatible with the official community plan. It advances the goals, which is to increase density and diversity of housing in all the neighborhoods of Saskatoon. We respectfully request the council to grant this rezoning this evening and show that adding additional new dwelling units to established neighborhoods is a good thing for the city of Saskatoon. That concludes my presentation. Thank you.

Thank you, Ms. Wallace. Are there questions of this speaker?

Councillor Senos Timon: Thank you, Mayor Cynthia Block. To this speaker, thank you for the presentation, Ms. Wallace. My question is regarding the concerns raised by the rezoning. It's about 69 responses to the concerns. What actions have you taken to address those concerns? I'm not at all opposing, but they're looking for solutions to work with them. What things have you done in response to those concerns?

I understand there were two meetings held with the development group and the community. Since the project hasn't actually been designed yet, there's an opportunity to work some of the concerns that were heard into the design. For example, the concerns about parking: there will be onsite parking. The concerns about waste management: there will be onsite waste management. We really don't agree with all of the concerns about traffic and parking becoming chaotic and so on. That's just simply not going to happen. That's actually not a medium-density dwelling, although it's considered by the city to be a medium-density dwelling. In most other cities, it's not medium density; it's still low density. So, I think I'm speaking a little bit on behalf of the development group, but they heard the concerns. In the design of their final project, they will accommodate the concerns that they heard where they can on the site.

Okay. So, thank you for that. My next question would be about the design. You talk about the design and that there is not much difference between four dwellings and six-unit dwellings. You referenced some other neighborhoods, and one of the concerns is really about the character of the neighborhoods. How do you reconcile that?

Well, there is no reconciliation, Councillor. In my opinion, we're following the official community plan, which is the guiding document that the city has approved for development of all neighborhoods in Saskatoon. What it states quite clearly is that all neighborhoods in Saskatoon should have a diverse range of housing types. In other words, what it's saying is exclusionary neighborhoods and exclusionary zoning are a thing of the past. It's not something that's a best practice any longer. The difference between a four-plex and a six-plex in terms of this location is negligible. I also want to address precedent: we hope there is a precedent here in that the city would consider accommodating six-unit dwellings on corner sites that are this large, or 18 meters or greater, because it just makes sense. Limiting it to the transit development area, although I can understand the rationale for doing that, I don't understand the rationale for eliminating that opportunity in the rest of the city. So that's why we're here tonight: it can establish a precedent, and maybe it should. That's what we're saying. Certainly, in this instance, this six-unit dwelling helps advance the housing goals, and it's in conformance with the official community plan.

Yes, thank you for that. I appreciate your response to that. One of my other questions would be around the financing. The administration mentioned the discussions that the group had with the administration regarding the compromise to four-plexes instead of six. But one of the things he indicated is that the group wanted these six-plexes because of the financing. So, is this more about the financing of the project rather than actually meeting the needs of the residents, who expressed clear consensus?

Yes, the land use decision shouldn't consider the financing of the project; that's not what the decision is about. But I can tell you that in speaking with the development group, they need the additional two dwellings to make this financially viable.

Good. Thank you. I'll just ask a couple of follow-up questions. So, are you saying, Ms. Wallace, that this project will not proceed without an approval of six units?

No, that question, I will have to ask Angie to maybe come up and answer.

Good evening, Your Worship and Council. My name is Angie Weeb, and I am one quarter of the purry for development group. In answer to your question about whether this project will proceed if it's four versus six units, we can't actually answer that at this time tonight. It's been a three-year-plus process, so we would have to revisit all of the numbers and look to see if that makes sense.

Okay. Thank you, Ms. Wallace. I had another follow-up question, I think for you, unless Angie wants to answer it. Can you just speak a bit more to precedent? You say that maybe there should be a precedent. What did you exactly mean by that?

Well, I think the city should look at not only accommodating six per corner in transit development areas, which I understand they're looking at. They've made that change, and then eliminating the opportunity elsewhere in the city because there are many, hundreds of properties that are immediately suitable for additional dwelling units on corner lots served on three sides by a roadway that have at least 18 meters of frontage. This site also has 32% more site area. The impacts of two additional units are not going to be felt; it just won't. I'd say that if it does establish a precedent, that same principle will carry through on all types of sites like this on corner sites. So, you may get another rezoning down the road. What I'm saying is rather than dealing with these one-off all the time, is to set a policy and allow for maybe even six units to be discretionary or permitted on large sites with 18 meters of frontage or greater.

Okay, I think I understand. Thank you. I don't have any other questions. I'm not seeing any other lights on, so thank you very much. We're going now to Janna Horn with the Holiday Park Community Association. Good evening, Your Worship and Councillors. My name is Janna Horn, and I'm the president of the Holiday Park Community Association and a homeowner on the 1300 block of 11th Street West. I want to thank you for your time to hear our concerns. As you heard this evening, we have had public engagement where 69 people had written in. They were handwritten letters; nothing was a form letter, and we wanted to highlight that tonight. From the engagement, you've heard the community has identified reasons for objecting to this rezoning as 'out of character.' A six-dwelling unit construction on a small lot is out of character for Holiday Park. It is common for us to see a duplex or two single homes built on a lot like this. But the proposed six-plex unit would be a very different type of development from the other infill housing projects that have been welcomed in our community of Holiday Park, setting a precedent for rezoning and demolition of our smaller homes. There are many smaller homes on lots which could become a target for demolition and high-density development by non-resident developers who set up their properties for quick sale or rental by non-resident landlords. Holiday Park is home to many of our smaller homes, and this is part of what makes our community unique and sought after as an affordable place for those who seek to own their own homes. Our community has a small-town feel where neighbors know neighbors, and this would be lost with such high-density development.

Parking space is a concern, and as someone who lives in the area, I'm well aware of this, especially in winter. The rezoning to RM2 to permit six dwelling units on a single lot will not leave room for off-street parking for six to 18 vehicles that would be typical of six households. This would present a hardship for existing residents as well as the six-plex residents, as on-street parking will be limited by the presence of the crosswalk. The corner of 11th Street and Avenue N is a busy crosswalk corner used by schoolchildren accessing their respective school that may not be in their neighborhood. Presently, Holiday Park has a Catholic and French school, and King George has the public school. If there are a lot of vehicles parked on 11th Street, it will affect visibility for turning traffic as well as pedestrians. A City of Saskatoon regulation will not permit parking within 15 meters before and 10 meters after marked crosswalks, which limits the on-street parking in this area.

Concerns exist with the existing narrow street of Avenue N and how increased traffic and on-street parking will impact the flow of traffic. Current residents find that vehicle use is pretty much required in Holiday Park due to the lack of local grocery stores and other services within a reasonable walkable or cyclable distance, as well as requiring multiple transit hops to reach places of work, grocery stores, and most other services that are not in Holiday Park. Regarding neighborhood safety, we reference the current ongoing concerns regarding safety, violence, assault, and high crime rates in the high-density Wellington Street and Embassy Drive apartment complexes. We do not want to see these types of safety concerns spread in our neighborhood. There are two senior housing complexes in our neighborhood, and already some of our residents have stopped walking in the neighborhood due to safety concerns.

Regarding waste bins, once a property goes over the four-unit dwelling, it becomes a multi-unit dwelling, and the regular garbage bins are no longer used. Instead, commercial garbage pickup is required. This is a huge concern as it would attract unwanted visitors. The Holiday Park neighborhood is unique as it's only accessible by traffic from two sides, unlike four sides in other neighborhoods. This puts additional strain on entrance and exit, and adding a multi-unit development will increase this pressure. If you look into the emergency service calls in Holiday Park, calls to the multiple-unit dwellings in the neighborhood are significantly higher in proportion to the calls to the R2-zoned properties in the neighborhood. Rezoning applications such as this one involve developers whose most important goal is to maximize return on investment, often failing to put the same importance on the impact on the surrounding properties, families, and neighborhood as a whole. We want to be abundantly clear to the City of Saskatoon that this is something we do not want in our Holiday Park neighborhood.

Thank you for your presentation. Are there questions of the speaker? Councillor Timon? Thank you. Through you, Mayor, to Ms. Con, I have one question in regards to the four-plex and six units versus four units. What has been the conversation with the CA in regards to the four-unit versus six? Should consideration be given for four units? Is that a concern still? We would wholeheartedly accept something if it was a four-plex due to things such as the waste bins; they would just have the regular bins instead of commercial ones. Things like that. The parking, those are the realities of winter, especially winter in Saskatchewan. Okay, so I have... thank you. I'm not seeing any. Maybe I'll just ask one follow-up just so I'm clear, Ms. Horne. You're fine with four units? We would accept that. Okay, and you are aware there could be multiple four-unit dwellings in your area? We understand that. Okay, all right. Thank you very much for your presentation.

Next, we have Homer Robinson. Mayor, Councillors, thank you for this opportunity to speak. I'm Homer Robinson, and I'm a member at large for the Holiday Park Community Association. We understand that it's financially advantageous to the developers to build a six-plex on the property at 1411 11th Street. However, this application for rezoning is asking the City planners to go against the policies that were established in the Housing Accelerator Fund amendments. The City planners have balanced the concerns of the people of Saskatoon with the growth plans for the city, and the resulting zoning guidelines that were developed are now in place. What's being proposed in their request to rezone 1411 11th Street is to go beyond what was allowed in the Official Community Plan and the Housing Accelerator Fund amendments. City Council and City Administration hold the big picture for development of the City of Saskatoon. We rely on City planners to provide guidelines and policies that promote safe and thriving communities that respect values in a neighborhood, and respect and value neighborhood relationships. Contrary to misinformation given by those who say that Holiday Park is not congruent with the diversity of housing forms, Holiday Park currently has a great diversity of housing and business types, including apartment buildings with 144 units, condos with 35 units, two seniors' complexes with 62 units, and many duplexes and double and single-unit homes. According to the latest 2023 City of Saskatoon Neighborhood Profiles, the number of renters in Holiday Park is almost equal to the number of owner-occupied homes, with 56% owner-occupied homes and 44% renter-occupied homes; essentially, almost half of the homes in Holiday Park are renter-occupied. There are only 10 communities in Saskatoon that have a higher percentage of renter-occupied homes than Holiday Park does. In other words, in Saskatoon, there are 53 communities that have many fewer renter-occupied homes than there are in Holiday Park. So, to sum up, it's important to maintain a balance of affordable homes that can be owned by occupants and homes available for rent. There are many development options that will provide a better infill fit in Holiday Park which do not require the rezoning. In addition to this background on Holiday Park, the current policy and guidelines provide specific reasons why a six-plex isn't suited to Holiday Park. Based on the Official Community Plan, the request to change zoning to RM2 does not comply in height and scale with buildings in the area. Number two, 1411 11th Street is not in the Transit Development Area. There's no policy that applies outside the Transit Development Area that would support the proposal. For those who say that 1411 11th Street is a larger corner lot, the lot is only 19 meters. There are several lots in Holiday Park on corners and mid-blocks that are similar. If this proposal to rezone to RM2 is approved, it would set a precedent for additional ad hoc zoning requests to build multi-unit type structures in Holiday Park. To grant this application would result in spot zoning, which by definition is when you change zoning for a specific property out of context with the surrounding properties and neighborhood. As explained in the March 31st Municipal Planning Commission meeting, it's important to avoid spot zoning so that there can be contiguous zoning in the neighborhood areas rather than having multiple unique properties with different zoning. If this application for zoning is granted, then there would be no policy evaluation criteria that could be applied to future rezoning applications in Holiday Park. Fairness and confidence in community development comes through the application of the policies and bylaws by city leadership. Consistency is important so that both developers and residents can anticipate what the city's position will be. We are asking the City Council to vote against the request to rezone 1411 11th Street West. Thank you very much, Mr. Robinson. Questions of the speaker? I'm not seeing any, but thank you again for taking the time to make your presentation. We're going to open it up now to see if there's anyone else in the gallery that would like to speak to this item. I'm not seeing any, so now we'll go back to ask questions of administration. I'll ask Mr. Dawson to take the microphone again and let Council ask questions of Mr. Dawson. If nobody has any, I might ask a couple. Mr. Dawson, I'll just ask a couple if nobody else has questions. Just for a bit of clarity. So, even if administration were considering bringing forth any kind of density changes on corners inside the transit corridor area, that would not apply in this case? That is correct, Mayor Block. This property is outside of the transit development area. So, I'll just forecast that next public hearing you will be seeing some amendments that are being brought forward by Planning and Development for the transit development area, to consider 60 units as a discretionary use. And they'll outline the policy and the reason why they're in the transit development area. As noted in my presentation, and by the speakers, this property is well outside of that transit development area or the core of growth area within the city's policies. Okay. Thank you. I think that's it for questions. Comments? Councillor Timon. Thank you, Mayor Block. I don't say thanks to the administration for presenting and working on this file, as well to pray for their work on this file. My understanding has been before my term here. So I had the opportunity to meet with the team and discuss the need, obviously of the infill, and also got to understand some of the concerns from the Community Association and also the residents who reached out to me. It's really important to address the challenges that we are facing in housing needs. And I see the need for development like this, but also I find myself in this place. We're trying to find the balance between the concerns from the community and also really the way you want to proceed. My understanding here is that the community is not all against this, but it just wanted to ensure that we are working within the policies that we have at the moment and also understand the need of the community. So I just want to say thank you for all the presenters who are here to pray for me, but I would say that I will not be supporting this application at the moment, knowing that there might be opportunity down the road. So, if the Pre-way for development decided to engage with the administration to consider the four-plex unit, that would be something that I'll be more comfortable supporting, I think. I don't see any highlights on. I'm going to ask someone to move a resolution to receive the report. It's just moved by Councillor Davies and Councillor Ford. Is anyone opposed? That carries. And a resolution to close the hearing moved by Councillor Dubois and seconded by Councillor Kelleher. Is anyone opposed? This is the last opportunity to provide any further comments, and I will just let Council know that movement of second reading carries this forward. A denial of moving forward with a second reading means it ends here. If there's any questions about that. Not seeing any, so I guess I'm asking for a mover for second reading. Does anyone want to move that? Mayor Block, I'm just flagging I had indicated a few minutes ago a question. I apologize, sorry. You sent me a note. I'm so sorry. Go ahead. Go ahead. My question was for administration, if that's acceptable. Okay, and if you could just speak up a bit or maybe we can bump your mic a bit. Sure. I'll just go ahead. Thank you. So my question for administration just had to do, generally speaking, if the lot in question here were subdivided into two separate lots, would they be able to get six units in two separate lots with, say, a main house area, a basement suite, and an accessory suite of some sort? Mayor Block, through to the Council. Thank you for the question. So if you have a lot that is 15 meters wide (which this one is 19), you could subdivide it into seven and a half where permitted in the zoning. And then you could build a one-unit dwelling with a secondary suite, with a garden suite, where allowed. One of the things that staff did look at after Municipal Planning Commission is whether this site could be subdivided. But I do want to answer it at a higher level on the ability for development. Where a one-unit dwelling can be built, you can have two secondary suites: one in the house and one as a garden suite. Perfect. So, at a very high level, it would be fair to say that in many cases you could have a similar sized lot or two lots, in fact, taking up the similar amount of area or frontage, that would ultimately be legally able to accommodate six units on two lots. Mayor Block, the hypothetical answer would be you could have one primary unit and two secondary units. So we would consider this accessory, but it does equal three dwelling units in total on a lot. For quick reference, building height in the R2, which as it currently is, is a half meter building height. RM2 is 10 meters building height for this particular site. So, a meter and a half difference. The site coverage is the same. So, the building height. There are other aspects such as gross floor area that apply in the RM2. But if we wanted to go just on building height and number of units, the site width limits the number of units in the RM2 as well as other zoning districts. And this would allow a meter and a half taller building height. Okay. Perfect. Thank you very much for that, Mr. Dawson. Okay. And in terms of making sure this is fair to everyone, we will consider that this resolution to close the hearing was halted when Councillor Davies signaled his intention to wish to speak that he wasn't able to previously. And I guess I'll just ask at this point if there are any. Before we go to second reading, I'll just ask again if we can get a resolution to close the hearing with all accounts. Moved by Councillor Dubois, seconded by Councillor Ford. Is anyone opposed? And hearing none, now we will go finally to the last opportunity to provide comments. Councillor Jeffries, would you like to speak to this? Sure. Thank you, Mayor Block, and just briefly. I provided this commentary at the Municipal Planning Commission, and just broadly speaking there, in many cases, there would be situations where the number of units and the amount of density that you might have on similar lots would, in fact, allow what the applicant here is looking for today. Certainly, I know we had something very similar come, I believe, last month. And one of the big differences I see between that and this one is we're talking about, I believe, RM2 versus RM3 requests that we had on the previous application that ultimately Council agreed with administration on and denied. So we're talking here about a lower level of that zoning and something that I think is more in line with potential max build out, which people tend not to do always. But it's more in line with what is existing in the neighborhood here, and for that reason, I am in support of the applicant's request and will vote against the recommendation of administration. Thank you, Mayor Block. Thank you, Councillor Jeffries. Are there any other comments? Seeing none, I will ask for a mover for second reading of the bylaw. Not hearing anyone willing to move second reading of the bylaw, Mr. City Clerk, my understanding is that means this is the end of the road. That's correct. So that is the ruling at this point, based on the information we had today. And I really appreciate everybody's involvement in this. If I've made an error in how this goes, somebody should tell me. I believe this matter has been concluded. Thank you to everyone who participated in the process. And we will now move on to 5.1.2, rezoning at 902 through 938 Third Avenue North from M1 District to CR2 District. If I could get a mover and seconder for first reading of the bylaw. Moved by Councillor Dubois and seconded by Councillor Donauer. Anyone opposed? That carries. Go ahead, Mr. Dawson. Thank you, Mayor Block. So this public hearing is to consider an application from Saskion Land to rezone 902 through 938 Third Avenue North in the City Park neighborhood from M1 Local Institutional Service District to CR2 Corridor Residential District. The subject properties, which are highlighted on the aerial photo on the screen, are located on the east side of Third Avenue North between Dutch Street and Duke Street and are currently undeveloped. So these subject sites are located in the corridor of Rotharia, specifically the wood lawn corridor plan area. As part of the Housing Accelerator Fund amendments approved in June 2024, the subject sites were redesignated from institutional to corridor residential use on the city's Official Community Plan land use map. The proposed rezoning to CR2, or Corridor Residential 2 District, is consistent with the corridor residential land use policies contained within the Official Community Plan. Just real quick, the purpose of the CR2 district is to provide for intensive occasion opportunities and support in the field development within the court of Rotharia in a range of ground oriented residential building forms, limited neighborhood commercial uses and related community uses and limited commercial uses. The CR2 district is intended to accommodate a transition between one and two unit dwellings and multiple unit and mixed use development. For reference, the zoning district would provide for building height of about a maximum of 15 meters, which would be typically four stories. In December of last year, a notice was sent to registered property owners and we went to our typical 150 meters of the site, the ward counselor and the City Park Community Association, and posted the information on the city's engage page.

5.2.1. Proposed lane closure, 1000 block University Drive. Could I get a mover for first reading of Bylaw 1070? Moved by Councillor Robert Pearce and seconded by Councillor Senos Timon. Is anyone opposed? That is carried. Go ahead, Mr. Schmidt. You've had a busy day.

Thank you, Your Worship and Councillors. My name is Terry Schmidt, General Manager of Transportation and Construction. Administration requests approval to close a portion of lane between 2011 and University Drive. Ronald McDonald House approached the City of Saskatoon about purchasing and closing this portion of lane. Purchasing this portion of lane would remove any safety concerns for guests walking between the house at 1111 and the outdoor area at 1117. A new lane will be constructed slightly to the east of 1119 University Drive to replace this closed portion. The existing lane begins at University Drive and is aligned north before taking a 90-degree turn and continuing east until ending at University Drive to the north of that segment. The lane currently operates with two-way traffic. All property owners on this block were contacted in November 2024 about the proposed changes. No objections were raised from any property owners. No compensation is required. The lane closure and replacement lane are equal in size. To complete this transaction, Administration requests City Council approve Bylaw Number 10170, the Street Closing Bylaw 2026, attached as Appendix 1. A turnaround area will be created at the west end of the east-west portion of the lane for westbound traffic. No legal access to parcels will be eliminated. Utility agencies have been contacted with respect to the closure. Rogers, Saskatoon Light and Power, and SaskTel have easement requirements. Communication activities are included in the requirement for public notice. No other communication activities are required. The applicant will be responsible for all costs associated with closing the lane, including, but not limited to, ISC fees, solicitors' fees and disbursements, decommissioning the existing lane, constructing the new lane, constructing the new median, and constructing the new turnaround area. There are three recommendations in the report for council consideration. I understand there may be representation here from Ronald McDonald House and their representatives, if there are any questions. Is that correct? Yes, it is. Thank you. That's my report, Your Worship.

Thank you.
